regimen_profiles.regimen_role: Chemotherapy before and after surgery for osteosarcoma
regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: Chemotherapy treats osteosarcoma cells throughout the body, including cells too small to see on scans, alongside surgery intended to remove the visible cancer.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: Chemotherapy before and after surgery for osteosarcoma
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Doxorubicin enters deoxyribonucleic acid, the genetic material called DNA, and interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme needed when cells copy and repair their genes. This damages tumour cells. Normal marrow, mouth and heart cells can also be injured. Cisplatin forms links within and between strands of DNA, the genetic material. These links stop cells copying their instructions normally. Kidney cells, the inner ear and nerves may also be injured, so prescribed fluids and organ checks are essential.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: Doxorubicin 25 mg/m² is given on days 1, 2 and 3; cisplatin 100 mg/m² on day 1. The reference course contains six 21-day cycles, usually three before surgery and three afterwards, with pathology review. Treatment dates and doses depend on recovery and the specialist plan.
key_points: This is the six-cycle doxorubicin/cisplatin course. It is distinct from the surgery-linked high-dose methotrexate combination. The national source gives no numeric age cutoff. Lifetime anthracycline exposure and individual heart risk must be reconciled.

regimen_profiles.regimen_role: High-grade osteosarcoma of an extremity or axial skeleton, excluding craniofacial sites, with all disease sites amenable to complete surgical resection; national eligibility age 40 years or younger
regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: The three medicines act through different mechanisms against osteosarcoma throughout the body. Surgery removes the visible tumour, and chemotherapy before and after surgery aims to reduce recurrence risk.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: High-grade osteosarcoma of an extremity or axial skeleton, excluding craniofacial sites, with all disease sites amenable to complete surgical resection; national eligibility age 40 years or younger
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Methotrexate blocks processes that use folate to make DNA, the genetic material. At this high dose it requires carefully timed folinic acid rescue to protect healthy cells. The kidneys remove methotrexate: slow removal can increase exposure and severe toxicity. Hydration, urine alkalinisation, blood levels and rescue are inseparable parts of treatment. Doxorubicin enters deoxyribonucleic acid, the genetic material called DNA, and interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme needed when cells copy and repair their genes. This damages tumour cells. Normal marrow, mouth and heart cells can also be injured. Cisplatin forms links within and between strands of DNA, the genetic material. These links stop cells copying their instructions normally. Kidney cells, the inner ear and nerves may also be injured, so prescribed fluids and organ checks are essential.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: The reference plan is not a repeating 21-day cycle. Before surgery, doxorubicin 37.5 mg/m² and cisplatin 60 mg/m² are each given on days 1 and 2 of weeks 1 and 6; methotrexate 12 g/m² is given on day 1 of weeks 4, 5, 9 and 10. Surgery is planned for reference week 11. Afterwards, doxorubicin is given on days 1 and 2 of weeks 12, 17, 22 and 26; cisplatin on days 1 and 2 of weeks 12 and 17; methotrexate on day 1 of weeks 15, 16, 20, 21, 24, 25, 28 and 29. Actual dates depend on surgery, recovery, drug clearance and safety review.
key_points: This course is limited to the stated age, site and complete-resection context. Up to two additional preoperative methotrexate doses may be prescribed if surgery is delayed. These are not automatic. Poor response on surgical pathology does not automatically justify adding ifosfamide/etoposide.
